title: Start With the Designer: A More Thoughtful Way to Discover Indigenous Fashion
subtitle: A useful guide to finding contemporary Indigenous designers, appreciating the clothes on their own terms and shopping with care.
imageAlt: Two friends browse contemporary garments together, looking closely at a jacket’s cut and fabric on a clothing rack.
imageConcept: A candid, warmly lit scene of two friends browsing a designer’s clothing rack at a fashion market or studio, comparing a jacket’s cut and fabric without costumes, staged cultural motifs or an implied lesson.
body: Begin with the clothes, not a presumed look

Indigenous fashion is not one silhouette, palette or set of motifs. It is contemporary fashion made by designers whose communities, experiences and creative choices are not interchangeable. Some work may draw on particular cultural practices; some may be streetwear, formalwear or pieces shaped by other influences. The first useful question is therefore not “What does Indigenous fashion look like?” but “Who made this, and what do they want us to know about the work?” That shift keeps the designer in view and makes room for the ordinary pleasures of style: proportion, color, texture, movement and construction. You can be curious without expecting a garment to explain an entire culture.
Browse from a source, not from a search for motifs

A more grounded discovery starts with designers, their own shops and profiles, or a Native-led fashion event. Those routes make it easier to connect a garment to the person or label presenting it, rather than to a vague online category such as “tribal-inspired.” If you encounter a piece through a retailer or marketplace, follow the trail back: Is the designer named? Can you find their own description of the work? Does the seller make a clear distinction between the designer’s work and something merely borrowing a visual reference? These are practical questions about authorship and context, not an invitation to investigate anyone’s private identity. Let the maker decide what information is public.

Recent fashion showcases offer a useful corrective to the idea of a single Indigenous aesthetic. An Associated Press report on a Santa Fe fashion week described collections featuring silk parasols, clothing and accessories made with materials ranging from wool trade cloth to animal hides, and contemporary streetwear, with designers from across North America [1]. That range matters: a shopper looking only for one recognizable motif may miss work that speaks through tailoring, material, color or a sharply modern silhouette. In 2025, Fashionista reported that more than 30 Indigenous designers convened at Native Fashion Week in Santa Fe [2]. Those examples are snapshots, not a definition of the field. Treat them as an invitation to follow individual designers and discover what each is making now.

When a piece catches your attention, pause on the designer’s product page or profile before forming a story about it. Look for the details a thoughtful fashion shopper would want anyway: fabric, construction, fit, care, sizing and how the garment is intended to be worn. Then read what the designer chooses to say about inspiration, technique or community. A description may offer important context, or it may focus on the garment’s material and making. Either is enough; no designer owes a shopper a cultural essay. Avoid treating a motif as a puzzle to solve or asking strangers to authenticate a meaning. If something is unclear, you can simply appreciate the design, seek information the maker has chosen to share, or move on.
Make browsing a shared style outing

For a simple two-person version, choose one event, designer profile or maker’s shop to explore together. Set a budget first if you plan to buy, and give each person a few minutes to browse independently. Each chooses one piece they genuinely like—not the most “representative” piece, or one they think the other person ought to choose. Compare what drew you in: perhaps a sleeve shape, a strong line through the shoulder, a fabric that holds its structure or a color that works with clothes you already own. Then check the designer’s own information for practical details. If the outing is online, open the designer’s site alongside the retailer’s listing. If you are at a market, let the designer or vendor set the terms of conversation; buying something should never depend on receiving a personal explanation.
Shop carefully without turning yourself into an investigator

Clear authorship and accurate seller claims matter. In U.S. guidance for buying American Indian arts and crafts, the Federal Trade Commission advises consumers to get written proof of claims about authenticity or origin and to make sure important information appears on the receipt [3]. That is a sensible consumer check when a seller makes those kinds of claims. It is not a reason to demand private identity documents from a designer, and it should not be stretched into a universal test for Indigenous identity or fashion. For any purchase, read the seller’s return, shipping and care information; confirm who is selling the item; and save the product description and receipt. If the language is slippery—if a seller uses a broad label while leaving the maker unidentifiable—ask a straightforward question about authorship or choose another source.
Wear the piece as clothing, with its context intact

A garment can be appreciated for its fit and still carry meaning beyond styling. If the designer describes a particular technique, collaboration or source of inspiration, keep that information attached to the way you talk about the piece; do not turn it into a claim the maker did not make. Be especially cautious about reproducing designs or symbols as a DIY project, or describing a piece as “traditional” when that is not the designer’s wording. In everyday wear, no special performance is required. Pair the garment with what you already like, follow care instructions and credit the designer when you share or recommend it. The aim is not to make the wearer the interpreter. It is to enjoy the work while leaving its authorship visible.

A thoughtful first visit does not need to end with a purchase or a perfect understanding. It can end with a designer whose work you want to follow, a garment you admired for its construction, or a question you can answer by reading the maker’s own materials. If you do buy, consider whether the piece suits your real wardrobe and budget; considered support is more useful than an impulse purchase made to prove good intentions. If you do not buy, you can still share the designer’s official shop or event information, accurately name the maker, or return when the timing is right. The point is to replace a search for one “Indigenous look” with attention to actual designers—and the many different fashion choices they make.
